Volume integral (∫V​fdV)

Words: 111 Articles: 1
Multivariable calculus OurBigBook.com
A volume integral integrates a scalar or componentwise vector field over a three-dimensional region with its volume form. In spherical polar coordinates the Euclidean volume form is r2sinθdrdθdϕ. The divergence theorem relates a volume integral of a divergence to a boundary flux integral.

Volume of a solid with affine thickness (V=Ah(x))

Words: 79
Volume integral OurBigBook.com
Let a bounded planar region D have positive area A and centroid x=A−1∫D​xdA. If a solid has nonnegative thickness h(x)=c+v⋅x above D, its volume integral gives
V=∫D​h(x)dA=A(c+v⋅x)=Ah(x).
(1)
Thus the average of an affine function over a region is its value at the centroid. The proof is the linearity of integration. For a disk the centroid is its centre, making the formula particularly useful for a cylindrical bore cut through a solid whose width varies linearly with height.

Fundamental theorem of calculus along a line segment

Words: 19
Multivariable calculus OurBigBook.com
If f:U→Rm is continuously differentiable and the segment from x to y lies in U, then
f(y)−f(x)=∫01​Df(x+t(y−x))(y−x)dt.
(2)

Partial derivative (∂)

Words: 2k Articles: 18
Multivariable calculus OurBigBook.com
A partial derivative measures the local response of a function to one input while its other inputs stay fixed. For a function f on an open subset of R2, its partial derivatives at (a,b) are the limits
fx​(a,b)=limh→0​hf(a+h,b)−f(a,b)​,fy​(a,b)=limk→0​kf(a,b+k)−f(a,b)​,
(3)
when the respective limits exist. Each is an ordinary derivative of a one-variable slice: x↦f(x,b) or y↦f(a,y). This is why the other variable is treated as a constant during partial differentiation.[ref]
For an original example, take the polynomial function
f(x,y)=x2+xy+2y2.
(4)
Holding y fixed gives fx​=2x+y, while holding x fixed gives fy​=x+4y. At (1,1), the height is f=4 and the two partial derivatives are fx​=3 and fy​=5. The values answer different experiments on the same mathematical model: change x alone, or change y alone.
The two exact slices through that point are
f(1+t,1)=4+3t+t2,f(1,1+t)=4+5t+2t2.
(5)
Dividing either height change by t=0 gives 3+t or 5+2t; taking the limit t→0 recovers the two slopes. At t=0.1, the finite height changes are 0.31 and 0.52, although their linear approximations are 0.3 and 0.5. A derivative measures the limiting response, rather than an exact finite change.
For a function of n variables, ∂j​f(a) varies only its jth coordinate: it is the same difference quotient along ej​, the jth standard basis vector. This gives a practical sensitivity analysis: one can compare how a mathematical model responds to changes in its individual inputs, provided the chosen system of units and the quantities held fixed are stated. Comparing the numerical sizes of two partial derivatives in different units does not by itself identify a physically preferable input.
Existence of the partial derivatives at one point is weaker than differentiability. The example under partial derivatives do not imply continuity shows how both coordinate tests can miss a bad diagonal approach. When the first partial derivatives are continuous in a neighborhood, they do give differentiability there, allowing the total differential to combine all small input changes.

Partial derivatives do not imply continuity

Words: 42
Partial derivative OurBigBook.com
Define f(x,y)=xy/(x2+y2) away from the origin and zero at the origin. Both partial derivatives exist everywhere and are zero at the origin, yet along x=y the function is 1/2, so it is not continuous there. Coordinate-axis derivative tests do not control all neighboring directions.

Mixed partial derivative (fxy​)

Words: 125 Articles: 2
Partial derivative OurBigBook.com
A mixed partial derivative takes partial derivatives in different variables, for example fxy​=∂y​(∂x​f). If both second partial derivatives are continuous in a neighbourhood, their order can be interchanged: fxy​=fyx​. The chain rule transforms mixed partial derivatives under a linear change of variables by composing the corresponding first-order differential operators.

Unequal mixed partial derivatives (∂y​∂x​f(0)=−1,∂x​∂y​f(0)=1)

Words: 39
Mixed partial derivative OurBigBook.com
For f(x,y)=xy(x2−y2)/(x2+y2) away from the origin and zero at the origin, ∣f∣≤(x2+y2)/2 proves Fréchet differentiability with zero derivative. Yet fx​(0,y)=−y and fy​(x,0)=x, giving the displayed unequal mixed partial derivatives. They exist but are not continuous at the origin, so Clairaut's theorem does not apply.

Symmetry of second derivatives (∂i​∂j​f=∂j​∂i​f)

Words: 43
Mixed partial derivative OurBigBook.com
When the second partial derivatives are continuous in a neighborhood, the order of the mixed partial derivatives can be interchanged. Expressing a rectangular finite difference as either iterated integral by the fundamental theorem of calculus and shrinking the rectangle proves the equality. Mere existence of both derivatives does not imply this symmetry.

Time derivative (∂t​)

Words: 31
Partial derivative OurBigBook.com
A time derivative is the partial derivative of an evolving field with respect to time while holding its spatial coordinates fixed. For a quantity depending only on time, it is an ordinary derivative.

Spatial derivative (∂i​)

Words: 11
Partial derivative OurBigBook.com
A spatial derivative is a partial derivative with respect to a spatial coordinate.

Directional derivative (Dv​f)

Words: 639 Articles: 5
Partial derivative OurBigBook.com
The directional derivative tests a function along a chosen straight line, including lines that follow neither coordinate axis. For a fixed vector v and a point a in an open subset of Rn, define
Dv​f(a)=limt→0​tf(a+tv)−f(a)​=dtd​f(a+tv)​t=0​,
(6)
if the limit exists. With a unit vector v, the parameter t measures signed distance in the input Euclidean space, so the directional derivative is change per unit distance. For a general v, it is change per unit parameter; the norm of v also sets the rate of travel.[ref]
For a differentiable real-valued function, the multivariable chain rule gives
Dv​f(a)=∇f(a)⋅v.
(7)
Thus one gradient predicts the local response in every direction. This formula requires differentiability, rather than merely separate partial derivatives.[ref]
Return to f(x,y)=x2+xy+2y2 at a=(1,1). Its gradient is (3,5). In the unit direction u=(3/5,4/5),
Du​f(a)=353​+554​=529​​.
(8)
One can check this without invoking the gradient formula: substitution gives
f(1+53​t,1+54​t)=4+529​t+2553​t2.
(9)
The difference quotient is 29/5+(53/25)t, whose limit is 29/5. This calculation separates the exact change along a finite path from its first-order rate at the starting point.
Changing the travel speed changes the parameter rate. Taking v=(3,4)=5u gives Dv​f(a)=29, because the input travels five distance units per parameter unit. For a differentiable function, Dcv​f(a)=cDv​f(a) for any real c: negative c reverses the orientation as well as scaling the rate. Normalizing v before comparing different slopes avoids confusing direction with speed.
The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality bounds the rate in any unit direction by ∥∇f(a)∥. Here the largest rate is 34​≈5.831, attained in the direction (3,5)/34​; the chosen (3/5,4/5) gives the slightly smaller rate 5.8. The perpendicular unit direction (−5,3)/34​ gives zero. That means no first-order height change, rather than no change at all: along this direction the example has f(a+tu)=4+(28/34)t2.
This is useful for following a height or temperature scalar field, choosing a local search direction in mathematical optimization, and distinguishing a coordinate sensitivity from a response along an actual path. For a curved path, derivative along a curve uses its instantaneous tangent vector. Even existence of all directional derivatives does not guarantee one common linear approximation; directional derivatives do not imply differentiability gives a concrete counterexample.

Gâteaux derivative (DI(v)[h]=limt→0​[I(v+th)−I(v)]/t)

Words: 52
Directional derivative OurBigBook.com
A functional on a Banach space is Gâteaux differentiable at v when the directional limits exist and form a bounded linear functional of h. Fréchet differentiability is stronger, requiring a remainder uniformly small compared with the norm of the increment. A quadratic norm bound on the Taylor remainder gives the stronger property directly. Mere existence of unrelated directional limits would not establish linear differentiability.

Finite increments of a logarithmic radial function (s=r0​(eΔ/2−1))

Words: 53
Directional derivative OurBigBook.com
For T(r)=ln∣r∣2, starting at radius r0​>0 and moving radially outward through distance s changes the function by Δ=2ln(1+s/r0​). Solving yields the displayed exact distance. Its small-increment limit is s≃r0​Δ/2, which is the initial directional derivative estimate. That linear estimate is not an exact equality for a specified finite change.

Radial derivative (∂r​u(x)=∇u(x)⋅x/∣x∣)

Words: 40
Directional derivative OurBigBook.com
Away from the origin, the radial derivative is the directional derivative along the outward radial unit vector. For a Sobolev space function it is the same scalar product with the weak gradient, defined almost everywhere. On an annulus, it has no singular direction at the origin.

Directional derivatives do not imply differentiability

Words: 53
Directional derivative OurBigBook.com
Define f(x,y)=x3/(x2+y2) away from the origin and zero at the origin. Every directional derivative exists. Along a unit vector n, the derivative at the origin is n13​, which is not linear in n. Thus these directional derivatives cannot be the restrictions of one Fréchet derivative, and the function is not Fréchet differentiable at that point.

Directional derivative of a convex function is sublinear (px​(y)=limt↓0​[f(x+ty)−f(x)]/t)

Words: 54
Directional derivative OurBigBook.com
For a locally Lipschitz function that is convex near x, increasing secant slopes have a finite right limit. Positive rescaling of t gives positive homogeneity in y. The convexity bound f(x+t(y+z))≤[f(x+2ty)+f(x+2tz)]/2 gives subadditivity after subtracting f(x), dividing by t and taking the limit. Thus px​ is a finite sublinear functional, although it need not be a linear functional.

Gradient (∇f)

Words: 440 Articles: 4
Partial derivative OurBigBook.com
In Cartesian coordinates on Euclidean space, the gradient of a scalar-valued differentiable function is the vector of its first partial derivatives. It converts a scalar field, such as temperature or a height, into a vector field describing its local change.
For a unit vector u, the directional derivative is Du​f=u⋅∇f. The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality gives ∣Du​f∣≤∣∇f∣. At a point where ∇f=0, the greatest increase per unit distance occurs along u=∇f/∣∇f∣, while the opposite direction gives the greatest decrease. These are first-order statements at the current point; they do not predict how the function behaves far along a straight path.
For f(x,y)=x2+2y2 at (1,1), ∇f=(2,4). Moving in the x direction gives rate 2 and moving in the y direction gives rate 4, but the steepest direction is (1,2)/5​, with
Du​f=25​​.
(10)
The direction (−2,1)/5​ has rate zero and is tangent to the level curve through that point. More generally, differentiating f(γ(t))=constant along a regular level curve gives ∇f⋅γ′=0, so the gradient is its normal vector.
This is useful when navigating a measured scalar field or applying gradient descent: one collection of partial derivatives predicts every infinitesimal directional change. The derivative assumes a differentiable function, not merely the existence of all directional derivatives. [ref].

Functional gradient (∇H​F(g))

Words: 69
Gradient OurBigBook.com
For a differentiable real-valued functional F on a real Hilbert space H, its functional gradient satisfies DF(g)[h]=⟨∇H​F(g),h⟩H​ for every h∈H. A bounded linear derivative has a unique such representative by the Riesz representation theorem. The inner product matters: a formal variational derivative need not equal the functional gradient in another Hilbert space. For F(g)=21​∑i​(yi​−g(xi​))2 in a Reproducing kernel Hilbert space, the reproducing property gives ∇H​F(g)=∑i​(g(xi​)−yi​)k(xi​,⋅). Substitution in the defining inner product proves this formula directly.

Gradient of a radial function (∇g(r)=g′(r)r/r)

Words: 96
Gradient OurBigBook.com
For r=x12​+⋯+xd2​​>0, the multivariable chain rule gives
∇g(r)=g′(r)r(x1​,…,xd​)​.
(11)
Indeed, ∂r/∂xj​=xj​/r. Thus the gradient points radially outward when g′(r)>0, inward when it is negative, and vanishes when it is zero.
At the origin the displayed quotient does not apply. If g has a finite right derivative at zero, the radial function is differentiable there exactly when g′(0+)=0, in which case its gradient is zero. Necessity follows by comparing opposite directional difference quotients: their linear parts cannot both equal a common nonzero radial slope. Sufficiency follows from g(r)−g(0)=o(r), the definition of differentiability with zero linear part.

Gradient of a dot product (∇(F⋅G)=(F⋅∇)G+(G⋅∇)F+F×curlG+G×curlF)

Words: 31
Gradient OurBigBook.com
For differentiable vector fields, expand the cross products using the contraction of two Levi-Civita symbols. The directional-derivative terms cancel the corresponding terms in the two cross products, leaving ∂i​(Fj​Gj​). This proves the displayed gradient identity by the product rule.

Gradient field

Words: 27
Gradient OurBigBook.com
A gradient field is a vector field of the form ∇f for a scalar potential f. Its curl vanishes wherever the required second derivatives commute.

Total differential (df)

Words: 286
Partial derivative OurBigBook.com
The total differential is the linear map that combines the first-order responses to simultaneous changes in all coordinates. For a differentiable real-valued function at a, it can be written
dfa​(h)=∑j=1n​∂j​f(a)hj​=∇f(a)⋅h,df=∑j=1n​∂xj​∂f​dxj​.
(12)
Here h is an input vector; dxj​ denotes the coordinate linear functional h↦hj​. The coordinate formula and the Fréchet derivative describe the same linear map. The defining approximation is
f(a+h)−f(a)=dfa​(h)+o(∥h∥)(h→0).
(13)
The little o notation says the remaining approximation error becomes small relative to the input norm, across every direction of approach.[ref]
For f=x2+xy+2y2 at a=(1,1), dfa​(h,k)=3h+5k. A simultaneous change (h,k)=(0.02,−0.01) gives the linear approximation
Δf≈3(0.02)+5(−0.01)=0.01​.
(14)
The exact algebra is
f(1+h,1+k)−4=3h+5k+h2+hk+2k2.
(15)
Consequently the exact change is 0.0104, and the approximation error is 0.0004. The total differential is useful for estimating the combined effect of small input changes without reevaluating a complicated function. For example, if ∣h∣≤0.02 and ∣k∣≤0.01, then ∣dfa​(h,k)∣≤0.11. These are deterministic bounds; a variance calculation additionally needs a joint probability distribution and its covariances. Hessian matrix (Hessf)

Words: 1k Articles: 11
Multivariable calculus OurBigBook.com
The Hessian matrix describes how the slope of a function changes in different directions. For a real-valued function f with continuous second partial derivatives on an open subset of Rn, it is
Hf​(x)=(∂xi​∂xj​∂2f​(x))i,j=1n​.
(17)
The symmetry of second derivatives makes Hf​ a symmetric matrix under these hypotheses. It is also the Jacobian matrix of the gradient: near x, a small displacement h changes ∇f by Hf​(x)h+o(∥h∥). Thus the gradient measures the current slope, while the Hessian measures its local variation. [ref]
For example, take the quadratic form
q(x,y)=x2+2xy+3y2.
(18)
Its gradient and Hessian matrix are
∇q=(2x+2y,2x+6y)T,Hq​=(22​26​).
(19)
The only critical point is the origin. Completing the square gives q=(x+y)2+2y2, so the origin is a strict global minimum. The eigenvalues 4−22​ and 4+22​ are both positive, recovering the same conclusion from the positive definiteness of the Hessian. Its eigenvectors identify the rotated directions in which the quadratic form has its smallest and largest bending.
For a fixed vector v, restriction to a straight line gives the directional interpretation
dt2d2​f(x+tv)​t=0​=vTHf​(x)v.
(20)
This is the quadratic form associated with the Hessian matrix. For a unit eigenvector v, it equals the corresponding eigenvalue. Opposite signs therefore mean that some directions bend upwards and others downwards. The second-derivative test turns this information into a classification when the gradient vanishes.
The same object is useful for computation. Newton's method in optimization chooses a displacement h by solving Hf​(x)h=−∇f(x) when the Hessian matrix is an invertible matrix; this makes the gradient of the local quadratic model vanish. For the displayed q, the equation gives h=−(x,y)T, so one exact step reaches the minimum from any starting point. For a general function, a Hessian with opposite-sign eigenvalues or a large condition number need not give a useful minimizing step, and the local minimum need not be a global minimum.
The name honors Otto Hesse. [ref] An older geometric use is the Hessian criterion for flexes of a plane cubic, connecting a determinant of second partial derivatives with inflection points of an algebraic curve. Hesse's 1844 paper Über die Wendepuncte der Curven dritter Ordnung is an early source on that geometric problem. [ref]

By Sylvester's law of inertia, the numbers of positive, negative and zero eigenvalues are unchanged. Independently of nondegeneracy, the local diffeomorphism preserves the critical point's status as a local minimum, local maximum or saddle point of a scalar function, because it maps neighbourhoods to neighbourhoods.

Second-derivative test

Words: 353 Articles: 2
Hessian matrix OurBigBook.com
Let f have continuous second partial derivatives near an interior critical point x∗​ of an open subset of Rn, with ∇f(x∗​)=0. The Hessian matrix gives the following sufficient conditions:
  • All eigenvalues positive: a strict local minimum.
  • All eigenvalues negative: a strict local maximum.
  • Both positive and negative eigenvalues: a saddle point of a scalar function.
A positive semidefinite or negative semidefinite Hessian matrix with a zero eigenvalue does not settle the classification. The higher-order test for separated extrema gives two quartic examples with exactly the same zero Hessian. These conditions apply to an interior critical point; a boundary optimum or a constrained optimization problem requires attention to the allowed directions. [ref]
The proof outline is the Taylor expansion
f(x∗​+h)−f(x∗​)=21​hTHf​(x∗​)h+o(∥h∥2).
(24)
For a positive-definite matrix, the smallest eigenvalue supplies a positive bound proportional to ∥h∥2, which dominates the remainder for small enough h. Negate the function for the local maximum case. For opposite-sign eigenvalues, choose the two corresponding eigenvectors: the leading terms have opposite signs along their lines.
There are also necessary conditions. At an interior local minimum, the Hessian matrix is positive semidefinite; at an interior local maximum, it is negative semidefinite. Restriction to each straight line reduces this to the one-variable second derivative condition. Since the Laplacian is the trace of the Hessian, it is nonnegative at such a local minimum and nonpositive at such a local maximum. The sign of the Laplacian alone is insufficient: x2−2y2 has negative Laplacian but a saddle point of a scalar function at the origin.

Nevertheless f(t,0)=t2>0 and f(t,t)=−t2<0 for t=0, so the origin is a saddle point of a scalar function. A valid second-derivative test needs a second-order Taylor expansion with a remainder o(x2+y2); continuous second partial derivatives in a neighborhood are a sufficient hypothesis. Existence of those derivatives at the point alone does not supply this hypothesis.

Critical points escaping to infinity in a Gaussian-weighted bilinear function (fα​(x,y)=xye−α(x2+y2))

The origin is a saddle point of a scalar function for every real parameter. For α>0 four further critical points have x2=y2=1/(2α). Their distance from the origin is α−1/2, so as α↓0 they escape every compact region. At nonpositive α the origin is the only critical point. This illustrates why the number of critical points on an unbounded domain can change without a finite degenerate critical point appearing.

Nondegenerate critical point

Words: 61
Hessian matrix OurBigBook.com
A critical point of a real function with continuous second partial derivatives is nondegenerate when its Hessian matrix is an invertible matrix there, equivalently when none of its eigenvalues is zero. A positive-definite matrix gives a strict local minimum, a negative definite Hessian gives a strict local maximum, and opposite-sign eigenvalues give a saddle point of a scalar function. A nondegenerate critical point need not be an extremum: x2−y2 has Hessian matrix diag(2,−2), which is an invertible matrix.
Such critical points are the local building blocks of Morse theory.

Vector calculus

Words: 9k Articles: 137
Multivariable calculus OurBigBook.com
Vector calculus studies differentiation and integration of scalar fields and vector fields. Three operators answer different local questions: the gradient describes change of a scalar value, the divergence describes net outward flow, and the curl describes local circulation. Their associated integral theorems turn local derivatives into measurements along paths and across boundaries.
The difference between divergence and curl is especially visible in two smooth vector fields on three-dimensional Euclidean space:
F(x,y,z)=(x,y,0),G(x,y,z)=(−y,x,0).
(26)
At each point they have the same Euclidean norm x2+y2​, but their directions differ. For F, ∇⋅F=2 and ∇×F=0. For G, ∇⋅G=0 and ∇×G=(0,0,2). One expands radially in each horizontal plane; the other describes rigid rotation.
Around the counterclockwise unit circle in the plane z=0, F is normal to the boundary and has zero tangential component. Its outward planar flux integral is 2π, while its line integral around the circle is zero. For G the values are reversed: outward planar flux is zero, and circulation is 2π. The divergence and curl predict exactly which boundary measurement survives.
Why is this useful? A velocity field can move material through a boundary or circulate it within a region. Conservation of mass connects its divergence with density changes through the continuity equation; its curl is vorticity. In electromagnetism, the Maxwell equations use the same operators to connect electric fields, magnetic fields, and their sources. The common mathematical language lets the same integral calculations work across different physical models. [ref].
The geometric framework behind these operators is developed in differential forms. The Generalized Stokes theorem unifies the fundamental theorem for line integrals, Green theorem, Stokes theorem, and divergence theorem. In coordinates their formulas look different, but each relates accumulation over a region to a measurement on its boundary.
Wilson's Vector Analysis, published in 1901, was based on J. Willard Gibbs's lectures at Yale. Wilson's preface explains that examples from geometry, mechanics, and physics are interspersed with the mathematical development, so readers encounter applications as soon as they have the tools to understand them. That is a useful way to approach vector calculus: learn each operation through a measurement it makes possible. [ref].

Laplacian (Δ)

The Laplacian takes the divergence of a scalar field's gradient. For a real-valued function f on an open region of Euclidean space, with continuous partial derivatives through order two, its expression in a Cartesian coordinate system is
Δf=∇⋅∇f=∑i=1n​∂xi2​∂2f​=tr(D2f).
(41)
Thus the Laplacian, also called the Laplace operator, adds the coordinate second derivatives; equivalently it is the matrix trace of the Hessian matrix. Its output is another scalar field.[ref]
Three original examples distinguish shape from this sum. The bowl f(x,y)=x2+y2 has Δf=2+2=4. The saddle g(x,y)=x2−y2 instead has Δg=2−2=0: opposite second derivatives cancel. It is a harmonic function, although its graph of a function is not a plane. For the Gaussian function h(x,y)=e−r2, with r2=x2+y2, differentiation gives
Δh=4(r2−1)e−r2.
(42)
Its Laplacian is negative inside the circle of radius one, zero on that circle, and positive outside it. The Gaussian function itself is positive throughout: its value and its Laplacian describe different properties.
The sum does not favor a particular orientation. Under a change of Cartesian coordinate system represented by an orthogonal matrix Q, the Hessian matrix becomes QT(D2f)Q. The cyclic property of the trace and QQT=I preserve its matrix trace. This makes the Laplacian useful when the behavior depends on spatial differences equally in every direction, rather than on the arbitrary choice of axes.
For a vector field, the Euclidean Laplacian acts separately on components expressed in a fixed Cartesian coordinate system. Components in a position-dependent basis require differentiating that basis too; applying a scalar formula separately to polar components omits those terms.[ref] The scalar formula in Laplacian in polar coordinates is valid away from r=0; smoothness at the origin must be handled in coordinates that remain regular there.

This is an asymptotic expansion, rather than an equality for arbitrary h. Rearranging gives the familiar central finite difference approximation

This finite difference replaces partial derivatives by five sampled values. The arithmetic mean lies above the center for a sufficiently small h if the Laplacian is strictly positive there, and below if it is strictly negative. A zero Laplacian cancels this second-order discrepancy without requiring equality of individual values.
At (0,0), the bowl x2+y2 has center value zero and four neighbor values h2, so the discrepancy is exactly h2. The saddle x2−y2 has neighbor values h2,h2,−h2,−h2, whose arithmetic mean is exactly zero. For the Gaussian function e−x2−y2 the discrepancy is e−h2−1=−h2+O(h4), agreeing with Δf(0,0)=−4.
A harmonic function need not equal this four-neighbor arithmetic mean for a finite h. The polynomial f(x,y)=x4−6x2y2+y4 has Δf=0 everywhere, but Ah​f(0,0)=h4. Higher-order terms remain even when the second-order terms cancel.
At a local minimum, each coordinate second derivative is at least zero, hence the Laplacian is at least zero. At a local maximum the inequality reverses. The sum alone does not characterize an extremum: cancellation at a saddle point of a scalar function can also produce zero. The local-average interpretation explains why the heat equation smooths differences, and helps motivate the heat equation maximum principle.

Thus a globally negative-divergence three-dimensional vector field has no such quasiperiodic invariant torus. This argument is stronger than merely noting contraction of transported phase volume; an attractor's own zero volume is not a contradiction.

Path independence

Words: 257 Articles: 2
Fundamental theorem for line integrals OurBigBook.com
A line integral is path independent when its value depends only on the two endpoints. On a connected domain, this holds for the line integral of every exact differential.
For a vector-field line integral, this condition is equivalent to the field being a conservative vector field.
Coinciding path integrals need not imply a conservative field
Words: 77
Path independence OurBigBook.com
Path independence requires the same line integral for every admissible path between fixed endpoints, not merely a few selected paths. For example, the smooth field F=(y−z,0,0) vanishes on the entire plane y=z. Every path in that plane from (0,0,0) to (1,1,1) therefore has zero integral. Yet the path through (0,1,0) and (1,1,0) has integral one: only the horizontal middle segment contributes. The curl is (0,−1,−1), confirming that the field is not conservative. Special paths can hide a nonconservative component.
Agreement of two path integrals does not imply conservativeness
Words: 138
Path independence OurBigBook.com
Equality of line integrals on two selected paths is a necessary test for a conservative vector field, but it is not sufficient. The paths may both miss the component responsible for nonzero curl.
For an explicit example, take W(x,y,z)=(z−y,x−z,y−x)T. Its curl is the nonzero constant 2(1,1,1)T, so it is not a gradient field on R3. Nevertheless, on the plane x=y, the field equals (z−x,x−z,0)T. Every tangent vector to that plane has equal first and second components, giving zero dot product with W. Thus every line integral of W along a path confined to that plane is zero, regardless of endpoints or the path's shape.
In particular, a broken straight path and a genuinely curved path in that plane can have matching line integrals while revealing nothing about global path independence. To establish a conservative vector field, construct a vector-field potential, or verify the appropriate global criterion such as zero curl on a simply connected domain.

Vector calculus OurBigBook.com
Green’s theorem converts circulation around a positively oriented planar boundary into the area integral of scalar curl.
Let D be a bounded region in the Euclidean plane whose boundary is a finite union of disjoint, piecewise smooth simple closed curves. Suppose the vector field F=(P,Q) is continuously differentiable on an open set containing the whole closed region. With positive boundary orientation,
∮∂D​F⋅dr=∮∂D​(Pdx+Qdy)=∬D​(∂x∂Q​−∂y∂P​)dA.

The partial derivatives Qx​−Py​ give the scalar curl: the third component of the curl of (P,Q,0). For a parametric curve γ(t)=(x(t),y(t)), the boundary line integral has integrand P(γ(t))x′(t)+Q(γ(t))y′(t).[ref]
Positive boundary orientation keeps D on the left as one walks along each boundary component: the outer curve is counterclockwise, and curves around holes are clockwise. Every component belongs in the line integral. The vector field must be regular throughout D, but need not extend into a hole.[ref]
The useful tradeoff is between boundary and interior: integrate tangential components along a curve, or integrate a partial derivative over a region, whichever is simpler. The boundary formula for planar area uses this freedom in the opposite direction, recovering area from a line integral. As a planar case of Stokes theorem, Green theorem also explains why a local curl can determine a complete boundary measurement while leaving room for the global obstruction in Green theorem with holes.
A short proof starts with a rectangle D=[a,b]×[c,d]. Add its four positively oriented edge line integrals:
∮∂D​(Pdx+Qdy)=∫ab​(P(x,c)−P(x,d))dx+∫cd​(Q(b,y)−Q(a,y))dy.
(75)
The fundamental theorem of calculus turns the differences into integrals of −Py​ and Qx​; Fubini's theorem then gives the required double integral. Each piece has a single simple closed curve as its boundary; along each cut, the two induced boundary orientations oppose, so those line integrals cancel when the two applications of Green theorem are added. Its inverse has Jacobian determinant 1/2, appropriate for converting area in the opposite direction. Writing down the map before computing its Jacobian matrix prevents a reciprocal-factor error.
Now reflect the image vertically: T(u,v)=(2u+v,−v) has Jacobian determinant −2, but still produces area two. The sign records reversal of the orientation of a vector space; ordinary area uses its absolute value. For oriented differential forms, the pullback of a differential form instead retains the signed determinant.[ref]
The geometric beauty is that a nonlinear differentiable map has a local linear approximation: tiny rectangles behave approximately like these parallelograms. Summing their scaled contributions gives the change of variables formula. In polar coordinates this factor is r, explaining dxdy=rdrdθ; equal angular steps cover more area farther from the origin. Inverse function theorem

Words: 2k Articles: 14
Differentiable map OurBigBook.com
The inverse function theorem answers a practical question: can nearby outputs be used to recover nearby inputs uniquely and smoothly? Its useful surprise is that a nonlinear function can be tested using its linear derivative. If the first-order changes preserve all input directions, then, on a sufficiently small region, the nonlinear map can also be reversed. This is the basis for treating a nonlinear map as a coordinate transformation.
Precisely, let f:U→Rn be continuously differentiable on an open subset U of Euclidean space, let a∈U, and put b=f(a). If Df(a) is an invertible linear map, there are open neighbourhoods U0​ of a and V0​ of b such that f:U0​→V0​ is a bijection with a continuously differentiable inverse function g. Thus this restriction is a diffeomorphism. In coordinates the test is detDf(a)=0, using the Jacobian determinant. The derivative of a local inverse map is obtained by inverting the Jacobian matrix, at the corresponding input. [ref]
For a one-dimensional example, f(x)=x2 has f′(1)=2. Near x=1, the inverse function is g(y)=y​, and the inverse function rule gives g′(1)=1/2. But x2 has no inverse function on the whole real line, since x and −x give the same output. The theorem supplies a local restriction, not global injectivity. At zero, the derivative test fails; the nonnegative branch still has a square root inverse, but that inverse has no finite derivative at zero. [ref]
Here is a two-dimensional example with an invertible derivative everywhere and infinitely repeated outputs:
f(s,θ)=(escosθ,essinθ),Df(s,θ)=es(cosθsinθ​−sinθcosθ​),detDf=e2s>0.
(111)
The exponential function turns s into a positive radius, while θ is the angle in polar coordinates. Restricting, for example, to ∣s∣<0.35 and ∣θ∣<0.6 produces the reversible patch pictured below. On its image, with Cartesian coordinates (u,v) and u>0, the inverse function is
s=21​log(u2+v2),θ=arctan(v/u).
(112)
The arctangent selects the angle near zero. Without an angle restriction, f(s,θ+2πk)=f(s,θ) for every integer k, so there is no single global inverse function. This map is a local diffeomorphism but is not injective.
The short proof idea is to correct a guessed input using the inverse linear response. With A=Df(a), solving f(x)=y is equivalent to finding a fixed point of
Ty​(x)=x+A−1(y−f(x)).
(113)
At a, the derivative DTy​(a)=I−A−1Df(a) vanishes. Continuity makes Ty​ a contraction mapping on a sufficiently small closed ball, which it maps into itself when y is sufficiently close to b. The contraction mapping theorem then gives existence and uniqueness there. Establishing the smooth dependence on y completes the inverse theorem. This explains why the nonlinearity can be tolerated: its correction has a small local slope.[ref]

Words: 317 Articles: 1
Inverse function theorem OurBigBook.com
The constant rank theorem separates the directions a smooth map preserves from the directions it forgets. If a smooth map from an open subset of Rm to Rn has derivative of constant rank r on a neighbourhood of a point, there are local coordinate transformations in source and target in which it becomes
(x1,…,xm)⟼(x1,…,xr,0,…,0).
(116)
It keeps r coordinates, discards the other m−r, and inserts n−r zeros. This is stronger than simplifying the Jacobian matrix at one point: it straightens the actual nonlinear map on a neighbourhood. [ref]
For a worked example, take
f(x,y)=(x+y,(x+y)2),Df(x,y)=(12(x+y)​12(x+y)​).
(117)
The two columns agree, and the first row is nonzero, so the rank is exactly one everywhere. The image of a function is the parabola b=a2. Every line x+y=a is a fiber mapping to the same point (a,a2).
Choose input coordinates u=x+y, v=x−y, and output coordinates α=a, β=b−a2. Both coordinate transformations are diffeomorphisms: their inverses are x=(u+v)/2, y=(u−v)/2 and a=α, b=β+α2. In these coordinates,
(u,v)⟼(u,u2)⟼(u,0).
(118)
The curved image has become a straight line, and the unused coordinate v is explicit.
Constant rank on a neighbourhood is essential. The map (x,y)↦(x,y2) has rank one when y=0 and two when y=0, so the constant rank theorem does not supply one rank-one form across that line. By contrast, the full-rank square case of the theorem forgets no coordinates and recovers the inverse function theorem. The usefulness is that curved fibers and images can often be studied through this simpler local form.

Local diffeomorphism

Words: 283 Articles: 2
Inverse function theorem OurBigBook.com
A local diffeomorphism is a differentiable map that restricts near every point to a diffeomorphism onto an open subset of its target. The local inverse functions need not combine into a single global inverse function: different parts of the domain of a function can map onto the same output region.
For continuously differentiable maps between open subsets of Rn, being a local diffeomorphism is equivalent to having an invertible derivative at every point. The inverse function theorem proves one direction. For the other, the chain rule for each local inverse function gives two inverse linear maps. The periodic angle example under the inverse function theorem has this property everywhere, even though it has infinitely many inputs for every point of the punctured plane. The noninjective map with constant Jacobian determinant gives another useful distinction: even a constant nonzero Jacobian determinant need not give global injectivity.
Every local diffeomorphism is an open map. To see this, take an open subset of the source and intersect it with the neighbourhoods where the map is a diffeomorphism. Each local image is open, and their union is the full image. Thus nearby outputs remain available locally, despite the possible global ambiguity.

A local diffeomorphism has both properties, but openness alone does not promise unique recovery of an input. In the periodic coordinate map under the inverse function theorem, open patches give open output regions while multiple angle values still give the same output.
Together, open and closed maps describe the two image-set preservation properties.

The implicit function theorem tells us when the constraint F(x,y)=0 determines y uniquely from nearby x, and makes the resulting function continuously differentiable. It is useful when solving an equation explicitly is cumbersome or impossible: the partial derivatives already reveal whether local recovery is possible.
Let F be a continuously differentiable map from an open subset of Rm×Rn to Rn. Suppose F(x0​,y0​)=0 and the partial derivative Dy​F(x0​,y0​) is an invertible linear map. There are open neighbourhoods U of x0​ and V of y0​ and a unique continuously differentiable function g:U→V such that, for (x,y)∈U×V,
F(x,y)=0⟺y=g(x),g(x0​)=y0​.
(119)
Thus the nearby level set is a graph of a function. The derivative of this graph is
Dg(x)=−[Dy​F(x,g(x))]−1Dx​F(x,g(x)).
(120)
The matrix inverse acts on the left; the order matters in several dimensions.
For example, take the unit circle, written as the level set F(x,y)=x2+y2−1=0. At (x0​,y0​)=(3/5,4/5), Fy​=2y0​=8/5=0, so the local upper branch is y=g(x)=1−x2​. Implicit differentiation gives
g′(x)=−Fy​Fx​​=−yx​,g′(3/5)=−3/4.​
(121)
This tangent line slope is available directly from the constraint. The negative square root branch is elsewhere on the same circle; it does not destroy uniqueness near the selected upper point.
At (1,0), however, Fy​=0 and the circle cannot be represented locally as one function y=g(x): just to the left of x=1 there are two nearby values of y. The circle is still smooth there. Since Fx​=2=0, use the other coordinate instead: x=h(y)=1−y2​, with h′(0)=0. A failed coordinate choice is different from a geometric singularity.
The derivative condition is sufficient, not necessary for every possible implicit graph. For F(x,y)=y3, the entire zero set is the smooth graph y=0, even though Fy​ vanishes there. In this case the defining equation itself has a degenerate derivative; the theorem's test gives no conclusion.
The connection to the inverse function theorem is particularly elegant. Augment the constraint to the map H(x,y)=(x,F(x,y)), whose Jacobian matrix is
DH=(IDx​F​0Dy​F​).
(122)
Its determinant is detDy​F. When this is nonzero, locally invert H and set its second output to zero. The recovered second input is g(x). In this way an implicit constraint becomes an ordinary inverse function problem. [ref]
Singular projection of an implicit curve
Words: 63
Implicit function theorem OurBigBook.com
For two constraints F(x,y,z)=G(x,y,z)=0, the implicit function theorem gives differentiable functions y(x),z(x) when the Jacobian determinant ∂(F,G)/∂(y,z) is nonzero. At its zeros this particular projection can fail even when a geometric curve remains. A nonzero tangent vector with zero x component gives a vertical tangent in that projection. Singular constraint representations require further care: a determinant of zero alone does not prove an infinite derivative or even a regular intersection.
Holomorphic implicit function theorem
Words: 36
Implicit function theorem OurBigBook.com
If a holomorphic function F(z,w) satisfies F(z0​,w0​)=0 and Fw​(z0​,w0​)=0, then near (z0​,w0​) its zero set is the graph w=g(z) of a unique holomorphic function. The analogous statement with Fz​=0 uses w as the local coordinate.
Implicit differentiation
Words: 158 Articles: 2
Implicit function theorem OurBigBook.com
Implicit differentiation differentiates an identity F(x,y(x))=0 along a differentiable branch and uses the chain rule to solve for its derivative:
Fx​+Fy​y′=0,y′=−Fy​Fx​​(Fy​=0).
(123)
The partial derivatives Fx​,Fy​ treat x,y as independent coordinates before evaluating on the branch. The implicit function theorem justifies the branch's local existence and regularity under its hypotheses; differentiating alone does not establish either. For the unit circle at (3/5,4/5), this calculation yields the tangent line y−4/5=−(3/4)(x−3/5).
Reciprocity rule for constrained partial derivatives ((∂y/∂x)z​(∂x/∂y)z​=1)
Words: 60
Implicit differentiation OurBigBook.com
On a regular level set F(x,y,z)=0, holding z fixed gives Fx​dx+Fy​dy=0. If F is continuously differentiable and both Fx​ and Fy​ are nonzero, the implicit function theorem gives (∂y/∂x)z​=−Fx​/Fy​ and (∂x/∂y)z​=−Fy​/Fx​. Multiplication proves the identity. The same held-fixed variable is essential, and a zero denominator invalidates the corresponding quotient rather than creating an infinite factor that may be cancelled formally.
Cyclic partial derivative identity ((∂x/∂y)z​(∂y/∂z)x​(∂z/∂x)y​=−1)
Words: 39
Implicit differentiation OurBigBook.com
On a level set f(x,y,z)=c, implicit differentiation gives the three ratios −fy​/fx​, −fz​/fy​ and −fx​/fz​. Their product is −1 wherever all the required coordinate representations are differentiable with nonzero denominators. At coordinate singularities the quotient product need not be defined.
